title: Ranbir Kapoor's Ramayana Is Now the Most Wanted Film in India. A $500 Million God Is Coming for Diwali.
excerpt: Nitesh Tiwari's two-part epic just overtook every blockbuster on BookMyShow's interest charts. With Hans Zimmer, A.R. Rahman, Dune's VFX house and a Ravana named Yash, this is India's audacious bid for its own Avatar moment.
body:
In a dimly lit studio outside London, a god is being assembled pixel by pixel. Ranbir Kapoor stands in battle armour, a cascade of digital light pouring over his shoulders, every glint on his sword rendered across servers strung between Vancouver, London and Mumbai. This is not a film set. It is a war room. And the man pacing it, Namit Malhotra, is betting close to half a billion dollars that the world is ready to meet Lord Ram on the same scale it met Iron Man.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=_oBCXJoka3s

This week, the gamble started to look like prophecy. Ramayana has quietly climbed to the very top of BookMyShow's interest charts — sitting at a staggering 67,600 registered interests, ahead of Shah Rukh Khan's King, ahead of Akshay Kumar's Bhooth Bangla, ahead of every glossy thing Bollywood is selling this winter. The film does not have a trailer in heavy rotation. It does not have a hit song dominating Reels. It has a teaser, a Diwali date, and an idea so large it makes everything around it look small.

"This isn't an Indian film. It's a global movie told through Indian eyes." — Namit Malhotra, producer

Let's talk about the spectacle, because the spectacle is the entire point. The combined budget across two parts is reported at roughly ₹4,000 crore — about $500 million — which would make Ramayana the most expensive production ever mounted out of India, by a distance that isn't even a contest. Kalki 2898 AD, RRR, Adipurush, Brahmastra — line them all up and they still don't reach this number. The visual effects are being handled by DNEG, the Oscar-winning house behind Dune and Interstellar. The music is a once-in-a-generation pairing: A.R. Rahman on the songs and Hans Zimmer on the score, the Dune and Interstellar maestro making his Indian debut. When was the last time a single film promised you Rahman and Zimmer in the same breath?

The casting alone makes this a must-watch. Ranbir Kapoor as Ram — leaner, stiller, more godlike than the rakish charmer the diaspora grew up on. Sai Pallavi as Sita, the most quietly luminous choice the makers could have made; there is no actress working today who radiates that particular warmth. And then the masterstroke: Yash, the KGF supernova, as Ravana. The man who taught a generation to cheer for a villain is now playing the most magnificent antagonist in Indian mythology. Sunny Deol roars in as Hanuman. Amitabh Bachchan, Arun Govil — the original television Ram, now passing the torch — Ravi Dubey as Lakshman, and a bench that runs to Rakul Preet Singh, Lara Dutta and Kunal Kapoor. This isn't a cast. It's a coronation.

Director Nitesh Tiwari knows about turning faith into footfalls — this is the man who made Dangal, the highest-grossing Indian film of its era. Producer Malhotra, whose Prime Focus has lost money in eight of the last ten years, is doing the opposite of de-risking. He rejected a record ₹700 crore OTT offer for both parts and is holding out for ₹1,000 crore, betting the world will pay more once it sees more. Audacity, or arrogance? With these numbers, there's barely a difference.

For the diaspora, the most fascinating reveal is technical. Malhotra has confirmed Ramayana will release not just with dubbing and subtitles, but with full lip-synced English, Spanish and Japanese versions, generated through cutting-edge AI — so that a kid in New Jersey or a family in São Paulo watches Ram's mouth move in their own language. "We can't bring Ram into the world sounding apologetic," Malhotra says. It is the single most ambitious distribution swing an Indian film has ever attempted: a simultaneous global theatrical play, pitched at Marvel scale, for a story older than every studio that ever tried to copy it.

Ramayana: Part 1 is locked for 6 November 2026, Diwali — and it is hurtling toward a clash with whatever Hollywood throws into the same window. For NRIs, this is the rare Indian release that won't arrive as an afterthought a week late; it's being built, from the servers up, to land in your local multiplex on opening night, in your language, at full volume. The interest charts already know. The only question left is whether the film can possibly be as big as the dream behind it.
